source.title: Speedy Performance Estimation for Neural Architecture Search
source.authors: Robin Ru; Clare Lyle; Lisa Schut; M. Fil; Mark van der Wilk; Yarin Gal

record.tranche_reason: Uses training losses and training speed to estimate architecture performance for NAS, but does not test the claim versions about training classification error.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training-loss behavior on NASBench-201, but does not report training classification error; the loss results cannot establish whether classification error reached zero.
record.test_reason: The study uses training speed and eventual small training losses to build and evaluate a NAS performance estimator. Its results do not establish near-zero training classification error or test the width, depth, initialization, stability-threshold, or batch-normalization comparisons in V1–V6. Training-accuracy rank correlations in Appendix C.3 do not establish absolute training error.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that sums of early training losses efficiently estimate final test-performance rankings under fixed training setups and can improve NAS speed or search quality. They acknowledge that validation accuracy eventually overtakes their estimators with sufficiently large training budgets. They do not conclude that training classification error reaches zero.
record.recipe_differences: Measures training-loss sums to estimate relative generalization performance across architectures; it does not test the claim’s training-error outcome or interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that training-loss-based estimator performance changes with training budget and dataset; estimator usefulness declines as training losses become very small, especially on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100.

fits_no_version.finding: Many NASBench-201 architectures attain training loss below 0.1 late in training on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100; on ImageNet-16-120, all retain high training losses at epoch 200 and none meet the paper's loss-based overfitting criterion.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the tested NASBench-201 training recipe, attainment of small training loss depends on the dataset and training duration.

record.problems: The relevant training-loss outcomes are not numerical in the supplied prose, and training loss does not establish training classification error. The text describes aggregate behavior across architectures.

untested.parts: Absolute training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100; corrupted or random labels; and comparisons establishing the stated size, stopping, or regularization conditions.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious local minima, and the effect of extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation with depth and its prevention by identity shortcuts or the specified alternative recipes.
Controlled initialization comparisons measuring training speed, signal propagation, or trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, transient loss recovery, curvature evolution, edge-of-stability behavior, and divergence.
Batch-normalization comparisons measuring training speed or learning-rate tolerance, including Fixup alternatives.

record.verdict_notes: Comparisons across DARTS depths and training recipes evaluate estimator rank correlation, rather than the optimization effects named in V3–V6. The catapult paper is cited to motivate discounting unstable early epochs; its stability mechanism is not tested.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, corrupted or random labels, and the stated model-size and training-duration conditions.
Spurious minima and student width relative to teacher width.
Depth, identity shortcuts, and training error comparisons.
Initialization effects on learning speed or trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability, loss recovery, sharpness, and divergence.
Batch-normalization effects on training speed or learning-rate tolerance.
